newsitem.title: USA: Greenspan Q&A -- Production, capacity use Part II.
newsitem.headline: Greenspan Q&A -- Production, capacity use Part II.

text.p: Following are excerpts from Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's question-and-answer session Wednesday with the Senate Banking Committee, after the second day of his semi-annual Humphrey-Hawkins testimony to Congress.

Sen. Shelby, (R-Ala) -- "Some of your written statement spends time explaining the significance of capacity and the utilization of that capacity ... Given technology, a strong dollar and increased trade activity, is it unreasonable to believe the denominator in that equation should not be limited to production capacity?"
Greenspan: "As I tried to outline in my prepared remarks, there is a significant distinction between physcial facilities ... and labor employment.

"One of the really fascinating characteristics of the data over the last several years is in the order books for capital equipment. Unfilled orders are falling quite dramatically relative to shipments, meaning that the lead time between order and delivery is becoming rapidly narrower.
"When demand changes ... your ability to put physical things in place has obviously increased quite measurably.

"In addition, the expense of trade throughout the world and the globalization has added to that ability to respond to demand, so that the actual physical ability from our capital stock has ... improved."
Sen. Shelby: How does that change the way that you and we interpret capacity utilization data?

Greenspan: "The figures that we publish for capacity utilization do not change. They are in effect stipulating what is the amount of gap between production and capacity as it is perceived at that time by the managers of those establishments.
"The difference is not in the measurment in the size of the gap, but the ability to change that gap, and that's what's important."
